prompt.brief: Design a controlled chaos-engineering platform that schedules approved fault experiments, limits blast radius, measures resilience hypotheses, and automatically stops or rolls back unsafe tests.
successSignals: Define experiment hypotheses, target selectors, fault types, blast-radius budgets, guardrails, stop conditions, approvals, and evidence.
Require isolated environments or explicit production consent, progressive canaries, health gates, leases, kill switches, and automatic cleanup.
Separate experiment control from fault agents, telemetry, analysis, and CI/CD gates; make runs idempotent and reproducible.
Explain customer-impact detection, agent failure, network partitions, secrets, auditability, observability, and manual-only fallback.

functional: Create hypotheses and experiments, approve targets, inject bounded faults, observe health, stop/rollback, and publish resilience results.
Support scheduled/CI runs, canary progression, network/CPU/disk/service faults, maintenance windows, owner notifications, and run comparison.
Provide signed agent enrollment, kill switch, immutable evidence, teardown verification, experiment deletion, and recovery after controller failure.
nonFunctional: Enforce blast-radius and health guardrails so approved experiments stop before breaching customer-impact budgets.
Run thousands of experiments across fleets and CI pipelines without a single hot key or unbounded synchronous work.
Do not lose committed state; make retries and duplicate events safe.
Degrade safely when downstream workers, caches, or external dependencies fail.
scaleAssumptions: 10k services, 1k concurrent experiments, and 100 CI pipelines
Partition by the primary tenant, user, item, or geographic key and isolate hot partitions.
Keep serving state bounded; retain raw events or durable records for replay and auditing.

deepDives.title: Consistency and idempotency
points: Keep the Controlled chaos-engineering platform commit authoritative; let derived projections converge with visible version and freshness.
Use idempotency keys, conditional Controlled chaos-engineering platform writes, event IDs, and versions so retries and replay are safe.
Return Controlled chaos-engineering platform version and observedAt so clients can reason about freshness.

deepDives.title: Partitioning and hot keys
points: Partition Controlled chaos-engineering platform by its primary read and write keys, then isolate hot tenants, users, items, or regions.
Bound Controlled chaos-engineering platform work with backpressure and queue isolation so one hot key cannot dominate the cluster.
Keep a replay or reconciliation path for Controlled chaos-engineering platform projection drift and partial failures.

deepDives.title: Failure and recovery
points: Serve the last acceptable Controlled chaos-engineering platform projection or an explicit degraded response when workers fail.
Retain durable Controlled chaos-engineering platform records for replay and make each downstream effect independently retryable.
Measure Controlled chaos-engineering platform latency, backlog, freshness, error rate, and correctness drift.

tradeoffs.title: Strong consistency versus throughput
tradeoffs.recommendation: Strongly protect the business commit and use versioned eventual projections for high-volume reads.
tradeoffs.caution: Making every derived read synchronous increases coordination and tail latency.

tradeoffs.title: Push versus pull processing
tradeoffs.recommendation: Push bounded events to workers and pull durable snapshots on reads or recovery.
tradeoffs.caution: Unbounded fanout or full scans make bursts and hot keys expensive.

tradeoffs.title: Managed service versus custom control
tradeoffs.recommendation: Start with managed primitives where their limits match the access pattern, then isolate replaceable interfaces.
tradeoffs.caution: Provider defaults do not remove the need for quotas, replay, observability, and data lifecycle design.

commonMistakes: Putting all work on the synchronous request path.
Choosing a data store before writing the access patterns and consistency contract.
Ignoring retries, duplicate events, late data, deletion, privacy, or authorization.
Leaving hot partitions, backpressure, stale reads, and recovery unspecified.
Allowing unbounded requests or exports to compete with normal traffic.

followUps.question: What happens when the primary worker is unavailable?
followUps.answer: Acknowledge only after the durable boundary, serve the last acceptable projection, queue retryable work, and replay or reconcile after recovery.

followUps.question: How would you support a tenfold traffic spike?
followUps.answer: Pre-scale partitions, apply admission control and backpressure, isolate hot keys, cache immutable snapshots, and make freshness degradation visible.

followUps.question: How do you verify correctness?
followUps.answer: Use idempotency metrics, version gaps, sampled source-to-projection comparisons, replay tests, and a shadow rebuild before repair.
